opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to look at it is not "which jobs disappear," but "which tasks inside a job get automated first." Almost every job is a bundle of tasks. Some are very well-defined, with a clear input, a clear output, and a way to check whether you got it right. Those are the tasks AI eats first, because that's exactly the setting where we know how to train models: give them a target, give them feedback, and scale up.

So you'll see it hit things like routine coding, translation, customer support, a lot of document processing, and junior-level analysis pretty early. Not because those people aren't skilled, but because the work is easy to verify. If the code compiles and passes the tests, you know it worked. That kind of feedback loop is exactly what reinforcement learning thrives on.

The jobs that last longer are the ones where the hard part is figuring out what the right problem even is. Things like deciding what to build, taste, judgment, negotiating between people with different interests, taking responsibility when something goes wrong. Physical jobs also take longer, honestly, because robotics is still much harder than software. Moving bits is cheap. Moving atoms is expensive.

From my own experience as an engineer, the change already feels real. A lot of the code I used to write by hand, I now describe and review. So the job shifts from "doing" toward "specifying and checking." I think that pattern will spread to many fields. One person with good judgment can supervise a lot of AI work, which is great for productivity. But it also means the entry-level path gets squeezed. Traditionally, you learned judgment by doing the grunt work for years. If AI does the grunt work, how do young people build that experience? I don't think we have a good answer yet, and I think society should take that seriously.

My overall view is optimistic but not naive. The total amount of value created will go up a lot. The question is the transition: how fast it happens, and whether people have time and support to move into new roles. Technology usually moves faster than institutions, and that gap is where most of the pain comes from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses which tasks and jobs may be automated first, but it does not predict that researchers will be replaced before infrastructure engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "replace" is the wrong frame for most jobs, at least in the near term. What's actually happening is that AI is replacing tasks, not whole roles, and different jobs are exposed very unevenly depending on how much of them is made of tasks that can be checked.

Let me explain what I mean by that. The jobs that are changing fastest right now are the ones where the output can be verified cheaply. Writing code is the obvious example, because you can run the tests. Summarizing documents, drafting emails, generating first versions of designs, doing data cleanup, answering routine customer questions: all of these have a clear notion of "did it work," and a human can review the result in a fraction of the time it would take to produce it. So those tasks move to the model, and the human shifts toward specifying what they want and judging what comes back.

The jobs that are more insulated are the ones where verification is the hard part, or where the work is mostly about taking responsibility. A senior engineer isn't valuable because they type fast, they're valuable because they decide what should be built and they own the consequences when it goes wrong. A doctor isn't just pattern matching on symptoms, they're accountable to the patient. Physical work in unstructured environments, like plumbing or elder care, is still very hard for machines, not because of intelligence but because robotics lags way behind language models.

Then there's a middle category I'd actually worry about most, which is entry-level knowledge work. Junior analysts, junior paralegals, junior developers. Those roles historically existed partly as training pipelines. You did the grunt work and learned the field by doing it. If the grunt work goes to AI, companies still need senior people, but it's less obvious how anyone becomes senior. I think that's a real structural problem that we haven't solved, and it's not something the technology fixes on its own.

One more thing I'd push back on is the assumption that fewer hours of work per task means fewer jobs. Sometimes it does. But often it means more work gets done, because things that weren't worth doing at the old price become worth doing at the new price. We saw that with software itself. Spreadsheets didn't eliminate accountants, they changed what accountants spend their time on and massively expanded how much financial analysis happens. I expect a lot of AI's effect to look like that, with the painful part being the transition, where the people who lose the old tasks aren't automatically the ones who get the new ones.

So if I had to summarize: AI replaces verifiable tasks first, it augments judgment and accountability, it struggles with the physical world, and the biggest risk isn't mass unemployment so much as a broken ladder for people trying to get into skilled fields.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will replace tasks before it replaces entire jobs. If your work is repetitive, follows clear rules, and is easy to check, a lot of it could be automated. But most jobs involve a mix of tasks, so even when AI takes over part of the work, you may still need a person to make decisions, handle exceptions, and take responsibility.

And I don’t think the distinction is simply between creative work and routine work. AI can help write or design, but understanding what someone actually wants—and deciding whether the result is appropriate—is a different challenge. Meanwhile, some physical jobs might be harder to automate because the environment keeps changing.

So I expect different jobs to change at different speeds. Some roles will disappear, some will become smaller, and new roles will emerge. The big question is how we help people make that transition, because having new jobs eventually doesn’t automatically help someone whose job disappears today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI will replace certain tasks before it replaces entire jobs. Work that is repetitive, predictable, and easy to check is more likely to be automated. That includes some administrative work, data entry, and parts of customer service. But even in jobs like programming or design, AI can take over pieces of the process, so the impact won’t be limited to one type of worker.

The harder jobs to replace are those that require trust, responsibility, human relationships, or adapting to unpredictable situations. Even there, AI may change how people work. A teacher, for example, might use AI to prepare materials while spending more time helping individual students.

So I wouldn’t frame it as a simple division between jobs that disappear and jobs that are safe. Most jobs contain a mix of tasks. The big question is how quickly those tasks change, and whether people have the support and opportunities to adapt.
